candidates.draft_body:

'And the words of Esau, her elder son, were told to Rebecca in a dream, and Rebecca sent and called Jacob her younger son, and said unto him: behold, Esau thy brother will take vengeance on thee so as to kill thee' — Jubilees uniquely makes Rebekah's foreknowledge of Esau's murderous plot a divinely-given dream, not mere intuition. The Tewahedo dream-discernment tradition (the matriarchal-prophetic dream that saves the patriarch is a recognized canonical category) draws warrant: legitimate dreams from God can be relied on for major decisions when corroborated by the dreamer's righteous standing and the moral content of the dream. Rebekah's dream meets both tests.

candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 27:19 (Jacob's flight and Bethel vision (27:19)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And he dreamt that night, and behold, a ladder was set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven, and behold, the angels of the Lord ascended and descended on it: and behold, the Lord stood upon it. And He spake to Jacob, and said: I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac; the land whereon thou art sleeping, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed after thee' — Jubilees preserves the Bethel ladder vision of Gen 28:12-13. Tewahedo Marian-typology reads Jacob's ladder as the canonical OT image of Mary as the ladder-between-heaven-and-earth; the Wǝddase Maryam (Praise of Mary) explicitly invokes 'Mary the ladder of Jacob' in the Monday-evening cycle. The angels-ascending-and-descending detail is the canonical proof-text for the Tewahedo doctrine that angels are not static but actively traffic between heaven and earth on behalf of the elect (Heb 1:14 picks this up apostolically).

'And he set his face toward Haran, and he was alone in the way, and he travelled three days, and went to Lūz... And he tarried there one night, and he took a stone of the place and set it under his head, and he was alone in the place, and there was none with him' — Jacob's departure to Haran. Tewahedo monastic-pilgrimage theology preserves the alone-with-stone-pillow image as the canonical pattern of the ascetic's solitary travel: pillow of stone, hearing of theophany.

candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 27:27 (Jacob's flight and Bethel vision (27:27)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And Jacob vowed a vow, saying: if the Lord will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on, so that I return in peace to my father's house, then shall the Lord be my God, and this stone which I have set up as a pillar for a memorial in this place, shall be the house of God: and of all that thou givest me, I shall give the tenth to thee, my God' — Jacob's vow combines covenant-faithfulness, sanctuary-establishment, AND tithing. Jubilees uniquely treats the pillar (mäṣbäḳ) as legitimately establishable by the patriarch BEFORE any Mosaic-altar legislation; the Tewahedo täbot tradition (each Tewahedo church has its consecrated täbot — the tablet representing the ark) finds canonical anchor here: the sanctifiable-stone is a patriarchal-prerogative restored in the Tewahedo täbot. The tithe-of-everything-given is the canonical anchor for the Tewahedo ǝʾǝsär comprehensiveness (not just produce but all gifts received).
